newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stock index futures close mostly higher.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stock index futures close mostly higher.

text.p: U.S. stock index futures closed mostly higher, as traders and dealers covered short positions due to the relentless rally in the U.S. bond market, floor analysts said.
"It was thin down here, and the bond market caught shorts off guard," one floor source said.

Overall, concerns ahead of the U.S. December employment reports on Friday led to position-squaring. Traders said they want to trim positions in the event December nonfarm payrolls rise significantly more than 200,000, or significantly less.
Traders on average are looking for payrolls to rise 192,000, and are forecasting unemployment to drop to 5.3 percent, versus 5.4 percent in November.

Several floor traders said the March T-bond's rise through 111-12/32 increased the buying momentum in the S&P 500 futures market. Pull-backs in the contract were met with decent dealer buying, one trader said.

Arbitrage buy programs were reported in the afternoon, as March S&Ps maintained their 6.00-point-plus premium against the cash index. Fair value is at 5.10 points, and arbitrage sell programs were at a premium of about 4.50 points.
March S&Ps rose through Wednesday's pit high of 762.50 and plowed through a major resistance level at 763.50, a one-week high, before sliding slightly.

The contract verged on testing 764.50, which is a breakout level from a wedge pattern on the charts, technical analysts said. Above that level, resistance is at the one-month settlement high of 764.60.
Meanwhile, Nikkei futures remained sharply lower on underlying fears about Japan's economy. At the opening, March Nikkeis set a contract low at 18,171.0.

At the end of pit trade, March S&Ps were 3.40 higher at 758.90, New Composites were up 2.75 at 400.75, KCBT Value Lines rose 3.15 to 693.15, Nikkeis were down 445.0 at 18,265, Midcap 400s were up 1.70 at 261.85 and Nasdaq 100s were 2.25 higher at 865.00 ((Derivatives desk 312-408-8750;E-mail derivatives@reuters.com))
